title: Report on the Exchange Program
paragraphs: I am 服部智貴, a sixth-year student in the School of Medicine. I sincerely thank the doctors of the Frontier Association for their kind consideration in everyday matters. I was able to study abroad at the University of North Carolina (hereafter UNC) from March 24 to June 26. I sincerely feel this is entirely thanks to the professors of the International Collaboration Office, the people in the study abroad section, and the seniors of the Frontier Association who laid the foundations of study abroad. Thank you very much.

North Carolina is located in the southeastern part of the United States and is a state with a strong Southern character, where tobacco production thrives. Chapel Hill, the town where I was allowed to go, is very small and cozy, pleasant to live in, and surrounded by greenery, so it was an ideal place to concentrate on research and study. Many patients also spoke English with a distinctive Southern accent, and examining them was sometimes hard, but everyone was very kind, and it was a place where I felt human warmth, just as the phrase Southern Hospitality says.

During the three months I was given the chance to do clerkships in three departments: pathology, geriatrics and cardiology. In pathology I did clerkships for one week each in Frozen Section, GI, GU and Cytology. I keenly felt my lack of study in pathology, but the process of looking into the slides myself, asking about what I did not understand and acquiring knowledge was rewarding. In Gross Section, which is the making of specimens, I was allowed to work on the pathology of a case of systemic metastasis of melanoma originating on the sole of the left foot, in which amputation of the left lower leg had been performed for pain relief, and it was very shocking. I was also given the opportunity to give a presentation in English for the first time in my life, and I presented on a case of HNPCC, a hereditary colorectal cancer disease. However, I did not want it to be an ordinary presentation in which people just listen to excerpts from papers and guidelines, so I spared no time in building an original presentation with animation and my own interpretation, and I managed to get through the English of the presentation reasonably well.

In the next department, geriatrics, I did a very meaningful clerkship with the cooperation of Dr. 岩田勲, a graduate of Kyushu University. For the first two weeks I mainly accompanied him in examining outpatients. I was able to observe a wide range of outpatient settings, from ordinary clinics to nursing homes (CCRC) like super-luxury hotels. It was my first opportunity to talk directly with patients and do physical examinations, and both the results of what I had worked on in the pre-departure training and the parts where my practice was still insufficient came into relief. The practice in Japan was to master a general form and repeat a series of steps narrowing down the actual differential diagnosis. However, when it came to examining American patients in English, the first difficulty was getting them to understand what I was saying. The biggest cause was that my pronunciation and the rhythm of my English differed from those of the locals, but since the department I was in was geriatrics, the patients were hard of hearing and many had a Southern accent, so I think it was even harder. I also keenly realized how much I had been examining patients on the basis of only superficial medical knowledge until then. The flow and structure of history taking went well as practiced, but at first I could not at all dig into the patient's chief complaint, the thing that troubles them most, and from there grasp the whole picture of the patient. However, with the cooperation of the local medical students and residents, I think I became able to carry out the series of history taking and physical examination smoothly and accurately. I was also given the opportunity to be directly instructed by Dr. 岩田勲 in how to perform neurological physical examinations and cognitive function tests, which was very instructive.

In the second half of the geriatrics clerkship I was allowed to have inpatients on the ward, and this was quite hard. Basically I moved on the same schedule as the local students, so while getting through case conferences and lectures, I had to follow the course of my assigned patients' general condition and also check on my own which tests would be needed next and how the treatment would proceed, so there was a lot I could not do. Of course, I missed important parts of conversations on site, and could not attend the occasions when healthcare staff (residents and attendings) decided policy among themselves, and since not everything was written into the chart immediately, it was very hard. Even so, toward the end I felt I had become able to give presentations that reflected my own opinion. Here too, by looking for something I could do and tackling it actively, I was able to taste a sense of fulfillment and accomplishment. For example, when the ward pharmacist was absent I looked up the interaction between warfarin and a drug for prostatic hypertrophy and told the resident, thereby taking part in deciding the treatment policy, and because the patient's wife was from Italy and not yet fluent in English, I took over the telephone exchanges with the care facility. Believing that I, with the fewest duties in the team, could be most closely involved with the patient, I did many things. As a result I was able to build a relationship of trust with the patient, which also led to confidence in myself. It was a clerkship in which I truly learned a great deal from the patients.

In cardiology, where I rotated last, I did my clerkship in the CICU while going in and out of the cath lab to observe various cases. Here I did the clerkship together with an exchange student from China, and I was made to realize her wealth of knowledge and the depth of internal medicine. I sometimes felt a sense of inferiority. However, my own interest and enthusiasm for cardiology drew in many people and bore fruit in the best form: many irreplaceable encounters and education full of consideration and enthusiasm. What I learned most was that, by doing the clerkship over the long span of one month, I could follow the flow of deciding treatment policy in acute-phase treatment. Of course, in the clinical clerkships in Japan I had rotated through various departments and thought I had seen the decision-making process of healthcare professionals. But I learned the power of "reading the present situation and what lies beyond": grasping Swan numbers, other test values and the patient's general condition, carefully investigating whether the patient is dry or wet and the possibility of infection, and judging what tests will be needed in the future, at what time intervals, and that once cardiac function has declined this far an IABP will become necessary. In addition, I was allowed to observe two cases of TAVR, transcatheter valve replacement, which was recently approved in Japan as well. Both cases took less than two hours, and the symptoms improved greatly after surgery with no complications; I was moved by the perfect technique. It was a harsh schedule of six days a week, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., but it was a month in which I fully enjoyed the busyness of cardiology, where to use one's head, and how cool it is.

Lastly, for these three months I had the chance to share a room with a Chinese-American named Albert. I would like to introduce him a little. He is a second-year UNC student who loves Japanese anime and is currently studying in a laboratory with many Japanese doctors. He was the best partner for me. When there was something I did not understand about medical knowledge or how to present, he carefully taught me; we talked passionately about the differences between Japanese and American culture and about politics, ate and slept under the same roof, and laughed together about trivial things, and he was the best of friends. He himself says he would like to do a clerkship at Nagoya University through the exchange program, and I hope we can talk about many things again in the near future.

My study abroad was possible only because of the support of many people. Thanks to the professors of the International Collaboration Office who supported and encouraged me when I faced difficulties even before going abroad, the Japanese doctors who looked after me, and the seniors who gave me advice on studying abroad, I was able to go to UNC. To repay this kindness, I intend to make even greater efforts than before and become a full-fledged doctor, and at the same time, in my small way, to do what I can so that the connections among juniors and local students, and the exchange between Nagoya University and UNC, become more active than ever.
I close by praying for the continued development and prosperity of the Frontier Association. Thank you very much.
